commentary.bottom_line: Twenty-one frameworks, guidelines, and commentaries endorse public transparency reporting on AI tools, but no supplied study tests whether such reports improve trust, accountability, or patient outcomes. A health system adopting this practice would be acting on expert consensus rather than on a measured effect.

perspectives.view: No supplied study tests transparency reporting, and none documents the hazard of opaque AI use. The support comes from frameworks, one consensus guideline, and commentaries, which GRADE treats as expert opinion. Certainty about any effect on trust or accountability cannot be rated.

One commentary on drafted portal replies proposes logging when drafting was used, how much clinicians edited, and downstream signals such as urgent visits within 24 to 72 hours. These logs could supply content for transparency reports. No supplied study shows that publishing such data catches errors before they reach patients.

A commentary on the EU AI Act proposes public reporting of algorithmic impact assessments and bias audits and compares this to financial disclosure. A regulatory discussion paper describes the argument that generative AI is too opaque for current device frameworks. Neither source reports a test of whether disclosure changes institutional behavior.

The HEAAL framework states that low-resource settings need infrastructure and technical assistance investments to adopt equity practices. The recommendation calls for reports tailored to patients, yet no supplied study examines whether such reports reach or are understood by patients with limited English proficiency or low literacy.

The CHAI playbook calls for trained staff assigned to defined governance roles. Producing and updating separate reports for patients, clinicians, and other stakeholders would draw on that staffing. No supplied study measures the cost, staff time, or update frequency needed to sustain such reporting.

commentary.research_gap: No study compares health systems or units that publish tailored AI transparency reports with those that do not. Useful designs would measure patient trust, clinician reliance and override behavior, complaint rates, and error detection, and would test the readability and comprehension of reports for each intended audience.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Whether patient-facing transparency reports are readable or useful to these groups is unknown, and translated and plain-language formats would need evaluation before a system assumes they work.
